1                                         STATEMENT OF ISSUE

2           Whether the Court should stay discovery pending resolution of Meta’s motion to dismiss,

3    which is potentially dispositive of the entire complaint and can be decided without discovery.

4                                             INTRODUCTION

5           Plaintiff’s opposition ignores the two-factor test used by courts in this District in consider-

6    ing whether to stay discovery while a motion to dismiss is pending. Courts in this District consider

7    (1) whether the motion to dismiss is “potentially dispositive” of the entire case, and (2) whether

8    the motion can be decided without the need for discovery. As Meta demonstrated in its opening

9    brief, both factors are satisfied here. Meta’s motion to dismiss presents multiple independent

10   grounds for dismissal of the entire complaint. For purposes of this motion to stay discovery, the

11   Court need not consider Meta’s arguments for dismissal based on the clear lapse of the statute of

12   limitations—even though that is fatal to plaintiff’s case—because it is effectively undisputed that

13   Meta’s arguments for dismissal on the merits entirely satisfy the test for a stay of discovery. All

14   four of plaintiff’s claims are subject to dismissal because plaintiff fails to identify any promise that

15   Meta supposedly broke, which dooms both plaintiff’s breach of contract claim as well as its re-

16   maining claims (all of which are derivative of the breach of contract claim). This glaring omission

17   easily satisfies the first factor. In response, plaintiff misapprehends the relevant standard—i.e.,

18   whether these arguments are “potentially” dispositive of the whole case—and instead discusses

19   whether the motion to dismiss is “likely” to succeed, which is not the question at this juncture.

20   And plaintiff does not even contend that discovery would be necessary to resolve those arguments

21   for dismissal, thus waiving any argument as to the second factor.

22          Plaintiff’s other arguments are meritless. Plaintiff’s suggestion that Meta somehow failed

23   to confer with plaintiff regarding the stay motion is belied by the declarations submitted by both

24   parties attesting that the parties discussed the proposed motion to stay during the Rule 26(f) con-

25   ference. See Dkt. No. 30-1 ¶ 3; Dkt. No. 32-1 ¶¶ 3–4. And plaintiff’s contention that the motion

26   is premature because there is no “particular or specific” need for a stay is likewise belied by plain-

27   tiff’s own actions. Meta moved to stay discovery after plaintiff proposed a discovery plan calling

28   for substantial completion of discovery by October 17, 2025—a mere three and a half months after

     DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S REPLY IN FURTHER SUPPORT OF MOTION TO STAY DISCOVERY

1    Meta filed the motion to stay. Though plaintiff may not have propounded (yet) the discovery

2    requests that it stated in late June were “forthcoming,” its proposal that discovery be substantially

3    completed in such a short period of time shows that Meta will soon be burdened by discovery if a

4    stay is not entered. Plaintiff’s apparent gamesmanship—holding its supposedly “forthcoming”

5    discovery requests in reserve so it could argue that Meta had “failed” to articulate a “particular and

6    specific” need for a brief stay of discovery—should not be rewarded.

7                                               ARGUMENT

8            A stay of discovery is warranted pending resolution of a motion to dismiss if (1) the pend-

9    ing motion is potentially dispositive of the entire case and (2) the court can decide the motion

10   without discovery. Pac. Lumber Co. v. Nat’l Union Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburgh, PA, 220 F.R.D.

11   349, 351–52 (N.D. Cal. 2003). Courts in this District, including this Court, apply this two-part

12   Pacific Lumber test in evaluating stay motions like this one. See, e.g., Hoopes Vineyard LLC v.

13   Cnty. of Napa, 2025 WL 41929, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 6, 2025) (Breyer, J.). 1

14   I.      Meta’s Motion to Dismiss Is Potentially Dispositive of the Entire Case

15           Meta’s motion to dismiss undoubtedly satisfies Pacific Lumber’s “potentially dispositive”

16   standard. See Dkt. No. 29 at 3–4. As explained, Meta’s motion provides multiple independent

17   reasons to dismiss each of the four counts of plaintiff’s complaint. Not only did the statute of

18   limitations for each claim lapse years ago, see Dkt. No. 25 at 6–7, but plaintiff’s complaint fails to

19   identify any promise that Meta supposedly broke, id. at 9. Those deficiencies are fatal to all of

20   plaintiff’s claims.

21           Plaintiff devotes the bulk of its opposition brief to arguing (prematurely) that Meta’s mo-

22   tion to dismiss should be denied. See Dkt. No. 32 at 3–8; see also id. at 6 (arguing that Meta’s

23   motion to dismiss the breach of contract claim is “likely to be dismissed”). That is incorrect; but

24   in any event, it is irrelevant to the present motion. As a court in this District recently explained,

25

27        Ledwidge v. Fed. Deposit Ins. Corp., 2025 WL 1370484, at *1 (N.D. Cal. May 12, 2025);
          Leonard v. CVS Pharmacy, Inc., 2025 WL 1266929, at *1 (N.D. Cal. May 1, 2025); Greenspan
28        v. Musk, 2024 WL 4933334, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 2, 2024); Yangtze Memory Techs., Inc. v.

1    “the inquiries into whether [defendant’s] Motion to Dismiss is ultimately successful and whether

2    Plaintiff may be granted leave to amend do not factor into this District’s Pacific Lumber factors.”

3    Garcia, 2025 WL 1755648, at *2; see also Leonard, 2025 WL 1266929, at *2 (“Plaintiff primarily

4    contends that Defendant has not met this factor because the MTD is unlikely to succeed, but like-

5    lihood of success is not the standard for a stay of discovery.”). The first Pacific Lumber factor

6    focuses on the scope of Meta’s motion to dismiss, not whether the motion will ultimately be

7    deemed meritorious after it is fully briefed. 2

8            Plaintiff incorrectly states that the Court must be “convinced that the plaintiff will be unable

9    to state a claim for relief” to issue a stay. Dkt. No. 32 at 4 (citing Hoopes Vineyard, 2025 WL

10   41929, at *1). In fact, the Ninth Circuit—in the decision cited in Hoopes Vineyard—did not hold

11   that a court must be “convinced” that a motion to dismiss will be granted before staying discovery

12   pending such a motion. See Wenger v. Monroe, 282 F.3d 1068, 1077 (9th Cir. 2002). Instead, it

13   merely held that a district court does not commit error if it enters a protective order because it is

14   “convinced that the plaintiff [would] be unable to state a claim for relief.” Id. In other words,

15   being “convinced” that the plaintiff fails to state a claim is sufficient, but not necessary, for a stay

16   of discovery. See In re Nexus 6p Prods. Liab. Litig., 2017 WL 3581188, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 18,

17   2017) (“Good cause for staying discovery may exist when the district court is convinced that the

18   plaintiff will be unable to state a claim for relief.” (citation modified)).

19           Plaintiff does not even try to argue that Meta’s motion to dismiss would not be “potentially”

20   dispositive of the entire case. Instead, it erroneously asserts that a different “framework” applies

21   under Rule 26(c). Dkt. No. 32 at 2. But it is undisputed that Rule 26(c) ultimately governs the

22   analysis. Indeed, Meta cites Rule 26(c) in its motion, see Dkt. No. 29 at 2–3, and the Pacific

23   Lumber test used by courts in this District flows from that Rule, see, e.g., Garcia, 2025 WL

24   1755648, at *1 (reciting both Rule 26(c) and the Pacific Lumber test). All of the arguments ad-

25   vanced by Meta in this motion are consistent with that Rule.

26

         dismiss before granting Meta’s motion to stay. Cf. Dkt. No. 32 at 3–4. Courts in this District
28       have stayed discovery before an opposition to the motion to dismiss has been filed. See, e.g.,

1    II.       Meta’s Motion to Dismiss Can Be Decided Without the Need for Discovery

2              As Meta explained in its opening brief, the Court can grant its motion to dismiss without

3    the need for discovery, satisfying the second Pacific Lumber factor. See Dkt. No. 29 at 4–5. Re-

4    garding this factor, plaintiff’s opposition solely discusses Meta’s statute of limitations argument

5    (see Dkt. No. 32 at 4–5) and does not contend that Meta’s merits-based arguments for dismissal

6    of the complaint would require any discovery. Nor would any discovery be required as to those

7    arguments, because (as explained in the opening brief) they rely solely on the allegations in the

8    complaint. Dkt. No. 29 at 4–5. Plaintiff has waived any argument as to this factor. See, e.g.,

9    Lansdown v. Bayview Loan Servicing, LLC, 2023 WL 2934932, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 12, 2023)

10   (“A failure to respond in an opposition to an argument constitutes waiver or abandonment, and

11   thus concedes the argument.” (citation modified)).3

12   III.      Plaintiff’s Other Arguments Are Meritless

13             Unable to satisfy the governing standard, plaintiff suggests several other putative reasons

14   why a stay should not be entered. All are baseless.

15             First, plaintiff’s suggestion that the parties did not meet and confer regarding Meta’s mo-

16   tion to stay discovery is without foundation, as shown by the declarations that both plaintiff and

17   Meta submitted to the Court. See Dkt. No. 30-1 ¶ 3; Dkt. No. 32-1 ¶¶ 3–4. As set forth in the

18   declaration attached to Meta’s administrative motion for relief from the case management sched-

19   ule, counsel for Meta informed counsel for plaintiff that Meta was planning to move to stay dis-

20   covery on June 26, 2025. Dkt. No. 30-1 ¶ 2. At the parties’ subsequent Rule 26(f) conference, the

21   parties discussed the motion, and plaintiff’s counsel stated that it did not agree to a stay of discov-

22   ery and would oppose the motion. Id. ¶ 3. Indeed, plaintiff’s counsel acknowledges as much. See

23   Dkt. No. 32-1 ¶¶ 3–4.4

24

25   3
            To the extent the Court considers additional factors, those also favor staying discovery. See
26          Dkt. No. 29 at 5. Plaintiff’s generalized reference to “fading memories and the loss of evi-
            dence,” Dkt. No. 32 at 8, would apply to any case, and plaintiff offers no explanation for why
27          a brief delay would be prejudicial to plaintiff here.
     4
            Plaintiff’s suggestion that Meta’s certification regarding its compliance with the meet-and-
28          confer requirement is somehow inadequate (Dkt. No. 32 at 2 n.2) is not supported by any au-
            thority.

1            Second, Meta need not wait for plaintiff to serve discovery requests to move to stay. Cf.

2    Dkt. No. 32 at 2–3. On June 30, 2025, plaintiff’s counsel informed Meta that it would be serving

3    “forthcoming” discovery requests. Dkt. No. 30-1 ¶ 4. The same day, plaintiff’s counsel sent Meta

4    its draft discovery plan, which proposed that substantial completion of document discovery should

5    take place by October 17, 2025. Reply Decl. of Andrew Yaphe in Supp. of Mot. to Stay ¶ 2. Given

6    plaintiff’s proposal that discovery should be substantially complete in less than three months—

7    even though it has not yet served discovery requests—it appears that plaintiff is holding its “forth-

8    coming” requests, Dkt. No. 30-1 ¶ 4, in reserve until after briefing on this motion is complete. In

9    any event, courts in this District have granted motions to stay discovery even where no discovery

10   requests had yet been served. See, e.g., Jacksonville Police Officers & Fire Fighters Health Ins.

11   Tr. v. Gilead Scis., Inc., 2022 WL 17418970, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 5, 2022) (rejecting argument

12   that motion to stay discovery was premature because plaintiffs had not yet served discovery and

13   explaining that “Defendants’ motion [to stay] was prompted, in part, because the parties raised

14   their dispute about the need for discovery prior to resolution of the [motion to dismiss] in their

15   case management conference statement”).

16           Third, plaintiff’s contention that Meta was required to set forth a “particular or specific

17   need” for a discovery stay (Dkt. No. 32 at 3) again departs from the governing Pacific Lumber test.

18   As a court in this District explained earlier this year, “[plaintiff] fails to cite any authority that a

19   ‘particular and specific need’ to stay discovery is a required showing for a defendant seeking a

20   stay of discovery, and [plaintiff] fails to locate this requirement within the Pacific Lumber con-

21   text.” Garcia, 2025 WL 1755648, at *2. In any event, as discussed above, plaintiff’s position that

22   discovery should be substantially complete in a mere three months in and of itself demonstrates

23   that a discovery stay is warranted while the Court determines whether plaintiff even states a claim

24   for relief.

25                                             CONCLUSION

26           For the foregoing reasons, and for those set forth in Meta’s motion to stay, Meta respect-

27   fully requests that the Court stay discovery pending a decision on Meta’s motion to dismiss.

 1          Plaintiff Iron Tribe Fitness (“Plaintiff”) respectfully submits this opposition to Defendant
 2   Meta Platform, Inc.’s (“Facebook” or “Defendant”) motion to stay discovery.
 3                                      STATEMENT OF ISSUE
 4          1.      Whether the Court should stay discovery pending the resolution of Defendant’s
 5   Motion to Dismiss.
 6                  ARGUMENT AND RELEVANT FACTUAL BACKGROUND
 7          Facebook overcharged thousands of its advertising customers during a four-year period,
 8   reaping what its own executives described as “billions” of dollars in illicit revenue. Plaintiff’s
 9   well-pleaded allegations are supported by reference to internal Facebook documents that make
10   clear that these revenues were caused by a clear deviation from the existing and expected
11   procedures for Facebook’s advertising auctions. That deviation resulted from a change to the
12   computer code implemented in the advertising auction process, and Facebook engineers worked
13   for months to determine what had caused Defendant’s advertising revenues to suddenly and
14   materially spike, and then worked to correct that coding change so that Facebook’s advertising
15   auctions would function the way they were supposed to. Rather than inform its advertising
16   customers of the issue and refund their money, Facebook concealed it and intentionally “slow
17   rolled” the fix so advertisers would not discover that they had been overcharged.
18          Plaintiff Iron Tribe Fitness, a small business that placed ads on Facebook during the Class
19   Period and was overcharged by Defendant, asserts claims for breach of contract, breach of the
20   implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, unjust enrichment, and violation of California’s
21   Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17200, et seq. Each of these claims
22   is subject to the notice pleading standards under Rule 8 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure
23   and, to survive Defendant’s motion to dismiss, the Complaint need only contain “a short and plain
24   statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2);
25   Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 663 (2009). Iron Tribe’s complaint more than satisfies the liberal
26   pleading requirements of Rule 8.
27          Defendant now improperly seeks to avoid its obligation to participate in discovery simply
28   because it has filed a motion to dismiss the Complaint. That motion is unlikely to result in the

 1   denial of any of Plaintiff’s claims, let alone the disposition of the entire action, and discovery

 2   should not be delayed for months until Defendant’s motion to dismiss is denied. Defendant’s

 3   motion to stay is contrary to the letter and intent of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. As

 4   numerous courts in this Circuit have repeatedly recognized, the “Federal Rules of Civil Procedure

 5   do not provide for automatic or blanket stays of discovery when a potentially dispositive motion

 6   is pending.” Palantir Techs. Inc. v. Abramowitz, 2020 WL 13548687, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 30,

 7   2020). Indeed, “[h]ad the Federal Rules contemplated that a motion to dismiss under Fed. R. Civ.

 8   P. 12(b)(6) would stay discovery, the Rules would contain a provision to that effect.” Gray v. First

 9   Winthrop Corp., 133 F.R.D. 39, 40 (N.D. Cal. 1990). Accordingly, Facebook’s motion is “directly

10   at odds with the need for expeditious resolution of litigation.” Id. For this reason, under Ninth

11   Circuit law, “[a] party seeking a stay of discovery carries the heavy burden of making a ‘strong

12   showing’ why discovery should be denied.” Id.1
13          Defendant fails to meet that “heavy burden,” and does not even present the Court with

14   correct framework for analyzing its motion. “Requests to stay discovery are governed by Federal

15   Rule of Civil Procedure 26(c).” Celgard, LLC v. Shenzhen Senior Tech. Material Co. Ltd. (US)

16   Research Inst., 2020 WL 7394456, *1 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 4, 2020) (“a motion to stay discovery is

17   tantamount to a request for a protective order prohibiting or limiting discovery pursuant to Fed. R.

18   Civ. P. 26(c)(2)”). As a preliminary matter, Defendant failed to certify that it conferred with

19   Plaintiff as required by Rule 26, which requires that any motion for a protective order “include a

20   certification that the movant has in good faith conferred or attempted to confer with other affected

21   parties in an effort to resolve the dispute without court action.” Id. Given that Plaintiff had not

22   yet served any discovery requests on Defendant when it sought to stay discovery, Defendant could

23   not have engaged in any good-faith discussion with Plaintiff regarding the burdens imposed by the

24   requested discovery or the need for relief therefrom. At best, this motion is fatally premature.2

26

28   as noted, it could not have addressed any discovery requests from which Defendant seeks

28
     at 40. Defendant argues the Court must take a “peek” at the merits of Defendant’s Rule 12(b)(6)

 1   motion in considering the motion to stay. Def. Br. at 3 (citing Ledwidge v. FDIC, 2025 WL

 2   885845, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 21, 2025)). But as some courts have recognized, because Plaintiff

 3   has not yet responded to the motion, the Court cannot, “by a ‘preliminary peek,’ assess the merits

 4   of the motion.” Singh, 2016 WL 10807598, at *2; Pac. Lumber Co. v. Nat’l Union Fire Ins. Co.

 5   of Pittsburgh, PA, 220 F.R.D. 349, 351-52 (N.D. Cal. 2003). However, even if it could take a

 6   “preliminary peek,” a stay is only appropriate when the Court is “convinced that the plaintiff will

 7   be unable to state a claim for relief.” Hoopes Vineyard, 2025 WL 41929, at *1 (emphasis in

 8   original). Here, a cursory review of the Complaint makes clear that Defendant’s motion to dismiss

 9   is unlikely to succeed.

10          A.      Defendant’s Statute of Limitations Defense Will Require Discovery

11          Defendant’s primary argument for dismissal is that Plaintiff’s claims are untimely because
12   Facebook finally stopped overcharging its advertisers in 2017. Def. Br. at 4. But California law,
13   which governs the claims of Plaintiff and the Class (¶ 60), provides that the statute of limitations
14   for all of Plaintiff’s claims does not begin to run until the plaintiff could have discovered the
15   misconduct at issue, and the discovery rule postpones accrual of a claim until the plaintiff discovers
16   or has reason to discover the cause of action. Norgart v. Upjohn, 981 P.2d 79 (Cal. 1999). The
17   discovery rule plainly applies under the facts here, as the claim could not have been discovered
18   before the expiration of the statute of limitations. Cover v. Windsor Surry Co., 2015 WL 4396215,
19   at *3 (N.D. Cal. Jul. 17, 2015).
20          The Complaint makes clear that Defendant’s overcharging of Plaintiff and the Class could
21   not have been discovered, absent the investigation conducted by counsel, which included the
22   review of non-public information. ¶¶ 9, 52. Moreover, the Complaint cites internal Facebook
23   documents showing that Facebook actively concealed its overcharging of its customers, including
24   by “slow rolling” the implementation of the necessary coding change to avoid detection. ¶¶ 10,
25   48-52. California law does not permit Defendant to evade legal claims simply by concealing the
26   facts supporting such claims until the applicable statute of limitations has elapsed.
27          In all events, as the case law makes clear, whether the discovery rule delays the start of the
28   statute of limitations is a question of fact requiring discovery. See, e.g., Fox v. Ethicon Endo-

 2   limitations defenses involving the kind of tolling allegations here present questions of fact that are

 3   inappropriate for resolution on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion. See, e.g., Antonick v. Electronic Arts Inc.,

 4   2011 WL 4501324, at *6 & n.6 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 27, 2011) (Breyer, J.). Defendant incorrectly

 7          B.       Defendant’s Other Motion to Dismiss Arguments Are Without Merit

 8          Next, Defendant asserts that the Complaint “does not identify any promise that Meta

10   plaintiff does not allege otherwise.” Def. Br. at 4. These assertions do not address Plaintiff’s

23
            The Complaint alleges that senior Facebook executives, such as the Company’s Chief
24
     Economist, are quoted at length in articles that explained Facebook’s “second price” auction

 1   process during the Class Period. ¶¶ 32, 33. The extensive media and academic discussion about

 2   how Facebook’s auctions were supposed to operate, which included statements by Facebook

 7          Based on those well-pleaded allegations, the Complaint asserts that Facebook either (1)

 8   breached its contract with Plaintiff and the Class, or, in the alternative, (2) violated the implied

 9   covenant of good faith and fair dealing, while also (3) violating California’s unfair competition

10   statute and (4) being unjustly enriched at the expense of the Class. McNeary-Calloway v. JP

11   Morgan Chase Bank, N.A., 863 F.Supp.2d 928, 948 (N.D. Cal. 2012) (plaintiffs satisfied

12   “relatively light” FRCP 8(a) pleading standard for UCL, implied covenant, and unjust enrichment

23   ¶72. For purposes of the Court’s “peek” at the merits of the motion to dismiss, that allegation is

 1   because platform did not provide proper advertising placement).

 2          Defendant’s argument that “the implied covenant claim fails for the same reasons as the

 3   breach of contract claim” (Def. Br. at 12) simply ignores the allegations supporting that claim, and

 4   the well-developed case law establishing that the implied covenant imposes the duty Plaintiff

 5   alleges was breached here. Gutierrez v. Wells Fargo & Co., 622 F. Supp. 2d 946, 954 (N.D. Cal.

 6   2009) (the contract and implied covenant claims could both proceed because defendant’s “measure

 7   of discretion must be exercised subject to good faith and fair dealing and not so as to maximize

 8   bank revenue”); Boobuli’s LLC v. State Farm Fire and Casualty Co., 562 F. Supp. 3d 469, 486

 9   (N.D. Cal. 2021) (denying a motion to dismiss implied covenant, UCL, and unjust enrichment

10   claims where plaintiffs alleged defendants failed to return excess premiums).

11          The breach of the implied covenant claim does not turn on a breach of an “express”

12   provision of the contract (indeed, that is why the covenant is “implied”) but instead serves to

13   protect the expectations of the contracting parties. See, e.g., Mahmoud v. Select Portfolio, Inc.,

14   2018 WL 278621, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 3, 2018).             Here, Plaintiff alleges that “[b]y first

15   overcharging Plaintiff and the Class, and then concealing the overcharges and failing to reimburse

16   Plaintiff and the Class for the overcharges, Facebook breached the implied covenant of good faith

17   and fair dealing inherent in the contracts” and “violated the reasonable expectations of the

18   members of the Class.” ¶ 77. Courts interpreting California law routinely find a breach of the

19   implied covenant in similar circumstances where one contracting party is provided with discretion

20   (like Facebook had in conducting advertising auctions) and abuses that discretion to the detriment

21   of the other (such as Facebook did here by overcharging advertisers). See, e.g., Lever Your Bus.

22   Inc. v. Sacred Hoops & Hardwood, Inc., 2020 WL 2465658, at * 6 (C.D. Cal. May 11, 2020)

23   (“where a contract confers one party with discretionary power…a duty is imposed to exercise that

24   discretion in good faith”).

25          Moreover, the breach of contract claim and breach of the implied covenant claim cannot

26   fail “for the same” reasons as Defendant asserts, and Defendant’s request to stay discovery can be

27   rejected for that reason alone. To the contrary, here, Plaintiff alleges not only a contractual breach

28   but that Facebook acted in bad faith by identifying the overcharges, and then “slow-rolling” the

10   the express provisions of the contract, and Defendant is therefore incorrect that those claims fail

11   for “the same reason” as the breach of contract claim. Indeed, courts routinely reject the notion

12   that UCL and unjust enrichment claims are duplicative of contract claims, including in cases

13   against Facebook alleging similarly improper treatment of advertisers as those alleged here. See,

17   claims could proceed because “[a] defendant is not entitled to have a cause of action dismissed for

18   failure to state a claim simply because it conflicts with another cause of action”).

19   III.   OTHER CONSIDERATIONS FAVOR DENYING A STAY

21   supposedly remains “in its infancy” and because Plaintiff failed to uncover Facebook’s secret

22   overcharges sooner. Facebook contends that Plaintiff will not be prejudiced by a further delay.

23   But the opposite is true. If anything, Facebook’s years-long coverup of advertising overcharges,

24   together with the challenges posed by fading memories and the loss of evidence with the passage

25   of time, favors against imposing additional delay. See, e.g., Lemmon v. Pierce Co., 2021 WL

26   5217291, at *1 (W.D. Wash. July 7, 2021) (motions to dismiss “are often unsuccessful and a stay

1                                     SUMMARY OF ARGUMENTS

2            The Court should stay discovery while it resolves Meta’s pending motion to dismiss the

3    complaint. In determining whether to stay discovery pending the resolution of a motion, courts in

4    this District consider two factors: (1) whether the pending motion is potentially dispositive of the

5    entire case and (2) whether the court can decide the motion without discovery. Meta’s motion to

6    dismiss easily satisfies both factors. First, Meta’s motion explains that there are multiple inde-

7    pendent bases for dismissing all four causes of action in plaintiff’s complaint, including because

8    the statute of limitations for all of plaintiff’s claims lapsed years before plaintiff filed suit and

9    because the claims all fail on the merits for several reasons. But the Court need not even evaluate

10   Meta’s compelling legal arguments at this stage, because it is clear that the motion (if granted)

11   would dispose of the entire case, and because the motion is based solely on the factual allegations

12   in plaintiff’s complaint (demonstrating that no discovery is necessary to resolve the motion). Ac-

13   cordingly, this is a quintessential case in which discovery should be stayed while the Court deter-

14   mines whether plaintiff has any valid claim. Nor can plaintiff claim that a short stay while the

15   motion to dismiss is pending would be prejudicial, given that plaintiff’s complaint pertains to sup-

16   posed conduct that (based on plaintiff’s own allegations) did not continue beyond 2017—yet plain-

17   tiff did not sue until nearly eight years later. Plaintiff should not be permitted to burden Meta with

18   discovery at this nascent stage of the litigation.

19                                             BACKGROUND

20           A. Summary of Allegations

21           Plaintiff Iron Tribe Fitness filed its complaint on April 11, 2025. See Dkt. No. 1 ¶ 14. The

22   complaint centers on allegations regarding Meta’s use of an auction process to allocate advertise-

23   ments. See id. ¶¶ 15–33. Plaintiff alleges that Meta changed its auction process in 2013 from a

24   “second price” auction to a “blended price” auction, which allegedly resulted in higher prices for

25   advertisers. See id. ¶¶ 7, 29, 34, 36, 48. The complaint alleges that Meta began rolling out a

26   change that “corrected” its auction process in 2017. Id. ¶¶ 45, 49, 50. The complaint asserts four

27   claims: (1) breach of contract, id. ¶¶ 68–73; (2) breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair

28

1    dealing, id. ¶¶ 74–78; (3) violation of the “unfair” prong of California’s Unfair Competition Law

2    (“UCL”), id. ¶¶ 79–84; and (4) unjust enrichment, id. ¶¶ 85–90.

3           B. Meta Moves to Dismiss the Complaint

4           On June 16, 2025, Meta moved to dismiss the complaint with prejudice under Rule 12(b)(6)

5    of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. Dkt. No. 25. As the motion explains, the complaint

6    should be dismissed in its entirety for multiple independent reasons. First, plaintiff’s claims are

7    all time-barred. Though each of plaintiff’s causes of action is subject to a four-year statute of

8    limitations, the complaint is devoid of factual allegations that any wrongdoing occurred after

9    2017—almost eight years ago. See id. at 6–7. Second, plaintiff’s claim for breach of contract fails

10   on the merits because plaintiff fails to allege any contractual promise that required Meta to use any

11   particular auction system. See id. at 7–11. Third, all of plaintiff’s remaining claims (for breach of

12   the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, under the UCL, and for unjust enrichment)

13   likewise fail, whether for the same reasons as the breach of contract claim and/or for additional

14   legal reasons particular to those claims. See id. at 11–15.

15          C. Procedural History

16          On June 27, 2025 the parties held their Rule 26(f) conference. Prior to that conference,

17   counsel for Meta had informed plaintiff that Meta intended to move to stay discovery. At the

18   conference, plaintiff stated that it would oppose such a motion. 1

19                                              ARGUMENT

20          As this Court has recognized, a district court has “wide discretion in controlling discovery.”

21   Renati v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 2019 WL 5536206, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 25, 2019) (Breyer, J.)

22   (quoting Little v. City of Seattle, 863 F.2d 681, 685 (9th Cir. 1988)). Pursuant to this discretion,

23   “[a] district court ‘may, for good cause, issue an order to protect a party or person from . . . undue

24   burden or expense,’ including by staying discovery.” Yangtze Memory Techs., Inc. v. Strand

27       agement conference. Plaintiff stated that it would not agree to such a continuance unless Meta
         would in turn agree that the parties could issue discovery. Meta has filed an administrative
28       motion to continue the initial case management conference. See generally Decl. of Andrew
         Yaphe in Supp. of Def.’s Admin. Mot.

1    Consult, 2024 WL 4950180, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 2, 2024) (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c)(1)). A

2    stay of discovery is warranted pending resolution of a motion to dismiss if (1) the pending motion

3    is potentially dispositive of the entire case and (2) the court can decide the motion without discov-

4    ery. Pac. Lumber Co. v. Nat’l Union Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburgh, PA, 220 F.R.D. 349, 351–52

5    (N.D. Cal. 2003). In applying the Pacific Lumber test, “the court must take a ‘preliminary peek’

6    at the merits of the pending motion to assess whether a stay is warranted.” Ledwidge v. FDIC,

7    2025 WL 885845, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 21, 2025).

8    I.      Meta’s Motion to Dismiss Presents Potentially Dispositive Arguments

9            Under the first Pacific Lumber factor, “the question is only whether [Meta’s] motion to

10   dismiss is ‘potentially dispositive of the entire’” case. Reveal Chat Holdco, LLC v. Facebook,

11   Inc., 2020 WL 2843369, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 10, 2020). Here, Meta’s pending motion to dismiss

12   provides comprehensive arguments that would be “potentially dispositive” of plaintiff’s entire

13   complaint, and thus this factor clearly favors a stay.

14           First, Meta’s motion to dismiss targets all four counts in plaintiff’s complaint, and estab-

15   lishes that each count should be dismissed for multiple reasons. See Dkt. No. 25 at 6–15. There-

16   fore, if the Court agrees with Meta’s motion-to-dismiss arguments, the motion “will dispose of all

17   claims.” Leonard v. CVS Pharm., Inc., 2025 WL 1266929, at *2 (N.D. Cal. May 1, 2025). “This

18   is sufficient to meet the first factor.” Id.; see also McMillian v. Musk, 2024 WL 2091377, at *2

19   (N.D. Cal. Apr. 16, 2024) (“[T]he dismissal arguments need only be potentially (as opposed to

20   definitively) dispositive of the entire case to satisfy that prong.”); Muhmoud v. City of San Jose,

21   2022 WL 16855573, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 10, 2022) (explaining that “likelihood of success is not

22   the standard for a stay of discovery” and the question is whether “if granted, [the motion] would

23   be dispositive of all claims”); Nelson v. F. Hoffmann-La Roche, Inc., 2022 WL 19765995, at *1

24   (N.D. Cal. Nov. 2, 2022) (“While the Court does not provide an opinion on the merits of the pend-

25   ing motion to dismiss, the Court finds it is possible that defendants’ motion to dismiss could be

26   dispositive of the entire case.”).

27           Second, a “preliminary peek” at the merits of the pending motion to dismiss confirms that

28   a stay is warranted. As noted, the motion explains that there are several independent reasons why

1    the entire complaint should be dismissed. It shows that all of the claims are subject to dismissal

2    because the statute of limitations for each lapsed years ago, as is plain from the face of the com-

3    plaint. See Dkt. No. 25 at 6–7. It also shows that the core claim—for breach of contract—should

4    be dismissed on the merits because plaintiff does not identify any promise that Meta supposedly

5    broke. The complaint lacks any allegation that Meta did not “calculate[]” the “amount [the adver-

6    tiser] owe[s] . . . based on [its] tracking mechanisms,” which is all that plaintiff alleges Meta was

7    required to do by the alleged contract. See id. at 9. Moreover, Meta never promised to use any

8    particular auction mechanism, and plaintiff does not allege otherwise. See id. at 8. This is fatal

9    not only to plaintiff’s breach of contract claim, but also its remaining claims (which overlap with

10   and are duplicative of its breach of contract claim). See id. at 11–15.

11   II.    Meta’s Motion to Dismiss Can Be Decided Without the Need for Discovery

12          The second Pacific Lumber factor likewise warrants a stay of discovery pending the reso-

13   lution of Meta’s motion to dismiss. Because Meta moves under Rule 12(b)(6), by definition no

14   discovery will be required for the Court to rule in its favor. See Tradebay, LLC v. eBay, Inc., 278

15   F.R.D. 597, 601 (D. Nev. 2011) (“The purpose of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) is to

16   enable defendants to challenge the legal sufficiency of a complaint without subjecting themselves

17   to discovery.”). Moreover, the requisite “preliminary peek” at Meta’s motion to dismiss, see Led-

18   widge, 2025 WL 885845, at *2, confirms that no discovery is necessary to resolve the motion.

19          First, Meta did not attach any documents to its motion to dismiss or otherwise raise any

20   factual issues, and instead relies solely on the allegations in the complaint. See Dkt. No. 25. Courts

21   faced with identical scenarios have found that this factor favors a stay of discovery. See, e.g.,

22   Reveal Chat, 2020 WL 2843369, at *3 (finding that “Facebook has satisfied the second prong of

23   the test” where “Facebook’s motion to dismiss is based solely on the allegations in the Complaint

24   and does not raise any factual issues”); Cellwitch, Inc. v. Tile, Inc., 2019 WL 5394848, at *2 (N.D.

25   Cal. Oct. 22, 2019) (second prong was met where “the Court only needs to look at the pleadings

26   in order to issue a decision about its motion to dismiss”).

27          Second, Meta’s motion turns on legal issues that do not require any discovery. Plaintiff’s

28   claims all fail in light of the language of the contract as alleged by plaintiff in the complaint—and

                                                     4
     DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S MOTION TO STAY DISCOVERY
     CASE NO. 3:25-CV-03281-CRB
      Case 3:25-cv-03281-CRB           Document 29        Filed 07/02/25       Page 10 of 11



1     which Meta does not dispute for purposes of the motion to dismiss. Dkt No. 1 ¶ 53; see Jarvis v.

2     Regan, 833 F.2d 149, 155 (9th Cir. 1987) (“Discovery is only appropriate where there are factual

3     issues raised by a Rule 12(b) motion.”). This factor also weighs in favor of staying discovery

4     pending a ruling on Meta’s motion to dismiss.

5     III.    Other Considerations Favor Staying Discovery

6             To the extent the Court considers other factors, they likewise favor staying discovery pend-

7     ing the resolution of the motion to dismiss. See Kincheloe v. Am. Airlines, Inc., 2021 WL 5847884,

8     at *2–3 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 9, 2021) (considering whether stay of discovery will “promote efficiency”

9     and “conserve the parties’ resources” in addition to Pacific Lumber factors). This lawsuit remains

10    in its infancy, and the Court has not yet entered a case schedule, meaning that any temporary delay

11    would not prejudice plaintiff. See, e.g., Ledwidge, 2025 WL 885845, at *4 (“[T]his lawsuit is in

12    its early stages, and the Court does not believe that a limited stay of discovery while the question

13    of jurisdiction is resolved will unduly prejudice Plaintiffs.”); In re Nexus 6p Prods. Liab. Litig.,

14    2017 WL 3581188, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 18, 2017) (a “limited stay of discovery does not unduly

15    prejudice plaintiff”).

16            In addition, plaintiff’s delay in filing this lawsuit belies any claim it might make of being

17    prejudiced by a brief stay of discovery. The complaint does not allege any wrongdoing over the

18    past seven years, and plaintiff waited until well after the limitations period on its claims had lapsed

19    to file suit. As such, it cannot complain of being prejudiced by a short stay of discovery now. See

20    Reveal Chat, 2020 WL 2843369 at *2, *4 (finding no undue prejudice where plaintiffs allegedly

21    “inexcusably delayed pursuing their claims that occurred five to eight years ago”).

22                                              CONCLUSION

23            For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court stay discovery pending

24    the resolution of Meta’s motion to dismiss. For the same reasons, Meta respectfully requests that

25    the Court also continue the initial case management conference until Meta’s motion to dismiss is

26    resolved, to conserve the Court’s and parties’ resources. See Micron Tech., Inc. v. United Micro-

27    electronics Corp., 2018 WL 7288018, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 16, 2018) (staying discovery and

28    continuing the initial case management conference pending resolution of the motion to dismiss).

1           Pursuant to Civil Local Rules 7-11 and 16-2(d), Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”)

2    respectfully requests that the Court grant a brief three-week continuance of the initial case man-

3    agement conference—from July 18, 2025 until August 8, 2025—so that Meta’s concurrently filed

4    motion to stay discovery, Dkt. No. 29, may be fully briefed in advance of the conference.

5    I.     FACTUAL BACKGROUND

6           Plaintiff Iron Tribe Fitness filed a complaint against Meta on April 11, 2025, bringing
7    claims for breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, viola-
8    tion of the California Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”), and unjust enrichment. Dkt. No. 1 ¶¶ 68–
9    90. On April 21, 2025, the Court set the initial case management conference for July 18, 2025.
10   Dkt. No. 11. On April 23, 2025, the parties agreed on a stipulated briefing schedule for Meta’s
11   motion to dismiss, which the Court entered the next day. Dkt. Nos. 17, 18. Pursuant to that sched-
12   ule, Meta filed its motion to dismiss on June 16, 2025. Dkt. No. 25. Plaintiff’s opposition is due
13   on August 15, 2025, and Meta’s reply is due on September 15, 2025. Id.
14          Counsel for the parties held their conference under Rule 26(f) on June 27, 2025. Decl. of
15   Andrew Yaphe in Supp. of Defs.’ Admin. Mot. (“Yaphe Decl.”) ¶ 3. Prior to the conference,
16   Meta’s counsel informed plaintiff that Meta intended to move to stay discovery pending resolution
17   of Meta’s motion to dismiss. Id. ¶ 2. Meta’s counsel further explained that, in the event that
18   plaintiff intended to oppose such a motion, a short postponement of the initial case management
19   would be warranted so that the motion to stay discovery could be fully briefed and submitted
20   before the initial case management conference. Id. On June 30, 2025, plaintiff stated that it would
21   oppose the motion to stay discovery and that it would not agree to the proposed three-week con-
22   tinuance of the case management conference unless Meta agreed that the parties could issue dis-
23   covery and also would agree to timely respond to what plaintiff described as “forthcoming discov-
24   ery requests.” Id. ¶ 4.
25          Meta has concurrently filed its motion to stay discovery pending resolution of its motion
26   to dismiss. As set forth in that motion, discovery should be stayed because the pending motion to
27   dismiss would be dispositive of plaintiff’s entire complaint, establishes multiple reasons for dis-
28   missal of each claim, and can be decided without the need for discovery. Dkt. No. 29 at 2–4.

1    Further, a stay would not prejudice plaintiff, particularly because plaintiff waited until well after

2    the limitations period lapsed to file suit. Id. at 5.

3    II.     ARGUMENT

4            The Court should grant Meta’s request for a brief three-week continuance of the initial case
5    management conference. Civil Local Rule 16-2(d) provides that “a party . . . may seek relief from
6    an obligation imposed by Fed. R. Civ. P. 16 or 26 or the Order Setting Initial Case Management
7    Conference” by describing the circumstances supporting the request, affirming the moving party
8    has consulted with opposing counsel, and proposing a revised case management schedule. Civ. L.
9    R. 16-2(d)(1)–(4). Here, the circumstances favor a brief adjournment.
10           First, continuing the case management conference until Meta’s motion to stay has been
11   fully submitted will promote judicial efficiency. Multiple topics to be discussed at the case man-
12   agement conference—including discovery and case scheduling—assume that discovery will be
13   going forward. But, as set forth in the concurrently filed motion to stay discovery, there is good
14   reason to hold discovery in abeyance pending the resolution of Meta’s motion to dismiss. See Dkt.
15   No. 29. It would be highly inefficient for the parties and the Court to discuss a case schedule and
16   discovery plan on July 18, 2025, only to reconvene three weeks later to discuss whether discovery
17   should be going forward at all. Holding the initial case management conference alongside any
18   hearing on Meta’s motion to stay discovery would streamline this process and would preserve both
19   the Court’s and parties’ resources. Moreover, the Court has not yet set any deadlines beyond the
20   initial case management conference, so no other revisions to the case management schedule would
21   be necessitated by the brief continuance sought by Meta.
22           Second, there is no prejudice to plaintiff if the case management conference is continued
23   for three weeks. Even assuming that plaintiff were to serve initial discovery requests directly after
24   the July 18, 2025 conference, Meta’s deadline to respond to such requests would be after the an-
25   ticipated August 8, 2025 hearing on Meta’s motion to stay. See, e.g., Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(A)
26   (providing party to whom request for production is directed 30 days to respond). Moreover, not-
27   withstanding its motion to stay discovery, Meta will serve its initial disclosures on or before the
